title: After Studying Abroad at Tulane University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study at Tulane University for three months from April 2013. When I landed in New Orleans, which has a unique atmosphere created by the mixing of the lively brightness of cheerful people and an exotic flavour, I could not imagine spending a quarter of a year somewhere in this city, but as I was kept busy with the daily clerkships, a month and then another month passed in the blink of an eye. Now, on the plane heading for Narita, I am looking back on this clerkship, feeling a little sentimental.

In the first month I trained in surgery (vascular, endocrine and pediatric group). I was put on a team of six, including residents, an intern and other students, and this whole team saw the patients of each attending. I went to the ward at 5 a.m., checked the charts and did medical interviews and physical examinations of the patients, and while preparing so that I could report to the resident, it was soon past 6 and rounds began. After that, if there was time we ate breakfast together and then moved on to the operating room or observing the outpatient clinic. In treating patients, work was efficiently distributed among the residents, interns and students who received guidance from the attending surgeon, and it was impressive that this not only resolved the uneven distribution of burden within the team but was also very effective for the education of each person. At first I struggled with listening, but I think the real pleasure of this surgery rotation was that, supported by the warmth of the team, I was able to go and learn actively.

In the second month I rotated through endocrinology and observed outpatient clinics of categories that do not exist in Japan, such as veteran and charity. It was interesting that I could check, as appropriate, papers and the latest guidelines on cases that interested me and follow how EBM is practised.

What I chose for the third month was emergency medicine. It was a clerkship that could really be called the culmination of this study abroad: I did the medical interview and physical examination of patients arriving at the 2 or 3 beds assigned to me, and reported to the resident or attending together with my own assessment. One can choose where to observe from three booths of different character: the MER, where highly urgent patients gather, the RTA, which mainly does triage, and the UC, which provides primary care, and since I wanted to see cases brought in by ambulance and, if possible, to be allowed to do suturing, I did all of my clerkship in the MER. It was a fully shift-based system of 12 hours at a time, with changeovers at 7 and 19 o'clock. Certainly there were waves of fast and slow within those 12 hours, but when there was time I could go to the other booths or discuss my own cases with the residents, and my satisfaction was very high.

Training in the same way as the local students in America, where medical education differs from Japan, was not easy for me, who always had the feeling "since I have been allowed to study abroad, I want to somehow perform well." Besides reviewing the textbooks and notes I normally use, I checked papers and guidelines as appropriate and asked questions of senior doctors and presented, but I cannot deny that some of it was mere self-satisfaction, and it was mentally hard to train in half doubt as to whether I was reaching the level required of students. However, perhaps because they sensed my attitude of trying to learn without compromising even on points that could be left vague if I used my mother tongue, I felt rescued, as if my efforts were being recognised, when the senior doctors answered even the most elementary questions properly and gave me the chance to observe surgery and do first touches. America, where the differences between interns, residents, fellows and attendings are clear and which in a sense has a strongly hierarchical colour, was attractive in that in the place of learning everyone is equal and opportunities are given to anyone who wants them.

During this study abroad I was made aware of the differences between Japan and America on various occasions, but the most impressive was the difference in the insurance system. By rotating through the emergency department this time, which is also "the window of medical care in society," I was able to catch a glimpse of the problems America faces now. A case in which an MRI could not be taken because the patient was uninsured and was left as he was, delaying the diagnosis. A case in which, because the patient had no financial means to receive treatment and also many complications, no department would accept him, and in the end he always had to rely on the emergency department. I had had doubts about the significance of a universal health insurance system in which the premise that the same quality of care is provided everywhere can hide differences in performance, but when I witnessed the present state in which the emergency department has become the safety net for patients who cannot receive even minimal medical care, I keenly felt the need to consider it from another viewpoint.

Not only the clerkship in the hospital, but also being able to interact with people with backgrounds different from my own was an experience made possible precisely because I stayed for a certain length of time, and I think that coming into contact with various cultures greatly influenced the formation of my values. I also learned that things I had taken for granted were not so for people of other countries, and I came to appreciate Japan's good points anew.

Looking back, from when I began studying English before being given this opportunity to study abroad until I finished this clerkship, I faced truly many walls. The TOEFL that I could not conquer, medical studies that did not progress as I wanted, and the first day, which I met with a vague anxiety about whether I could do the clerkship properly. I had prepared myself for the language barrier even before departure, but each time I realised that it was higher and thicker than I imagined and that there had been compromise in my attitude toward studying medicine until then, I keenly felt my own powerlessness and was close to giving up many times. However, by thinking about what needed to be solved and overcoming things one by one, I gained a sense of achievement, and it also led to confidence. "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step." Thanks to being allowed to study abroad, I was able to reaffirm the courage to take the first step and the importance of accumulating effort afterwards. I believe that when I become a doctor in the future, not fearing challenges and making an effort is how I will make use of this experience.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the doctors of Nagoya University, the doctors of the International Exchange Office and the academic affairs staff who supported this study abroad, the doctors and seniors of the Frontier Association who instructed me at the training sessions, and my classmates who encouraged one another and worked hard together. Thank you very much indeed.
